sections.title: Metro lines and the HÉV suburban railway
paragraphs: Budapest has four metro lines, M1 to M4. M1, the Millennium Underground Railway, is the oldest: it opened in 1896, runs under Andrássy út between Vörösmarty tér and Mexikói út, and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site that covers the Danube banks, the Buda Castle quarter and Andrássy Avenue. Its stops include Opera, Oktogon, Hősök tere and Széchenyi fürdő, so it links the downtown with City Park. BKK confirms that single tickets and passes work on it, and that you validate before you enter the platform area.

The other lines are M2 (Déli pályaudvar to Örs vezér tere), M3 (Újpest-központ to Kőbánya-Kispest) and M4 (Keleti pályaudvar to Kelenföld vasútállomás), which opened in 2014 and runs without drivers. Deák Ferenc tér is the transfer point for M1, M2 and M3. The HÉV is the suburban railway; its lines carry the numbers H5 to H9. Inside the Budapest boundary a normal BKK ticket or travelcard is valid on the HÉV, but a trip beyond it needs a suburban ticket. MÁV names the boundary stations as Békásmegyer (H5), Millenniumtelep (H6), Ilonatelep (H8) and Szabadságtelep (H9), and notes that H7 lies entirely within Budapest.

sections.title: Trams, buses and the night network
paragraphs: Trams do much of the sightseeing work. A 2017 guide from We Love Budapest describes tram 2 as running along the Pest embankment past the Great Market Hall, the Palace of Arts, the Chain Bridge and Parliament towards Jászai Mari tér. Trams 4 and 6 follow the Grand Boulevard, the semicircle that links Margaret Bridge and Petőfi Bridge through Pest, and reach Buda at Széll Kálmán tér in the north and Újbuda-központ (line 4) or Móricz Zsigmond körtér (line 6) in the south. Track works change these routes from time to time, as the 2025 Grand Boulevard renovation did, so confirm the current route in BudapestGO before you rely on a line.

On Castle Hill buses fill the gap: BKK lists buses 16, 16A and 116 at the upper funicular station, and trams 19 and 41 and buses 16 and 105 at the lower one. Trolleybuses also exist; BKK mentions lines 70, 78 and 79. At night BKK's night-transport page says tram 6 runs around the clock and names the 100E and 200E airport buses and numerous night bus services. The same page announces a reorganisation of night routes starting in summer 2026, and it does not say how the metro is replaced overnight, so plan a late journey in advance instead of assuming the metro will carry you home.
bullets: Use the stop name, not only the line number, when checking a route.
Tram 6 is the one tram BKK describes as running around the clock.

sections.title: Funicular, chairlift, heritage trams and boats
paragraphs: BKK groups several scenic services as special transport, and they follow their own ticket rules. The Buda Castle Funicular, in service since 1870, links Clark Ádám tér at the Buda end of the Chain Bridge with Szent György tér beside the palace. Only a funicular ticket is valid there, sold at its ticket offices and other designated locations or as an e-ticket, and BKK tickets and passes are not accepted. You validate at the machine as you cross the platform boundary and keep the ticket until you leave the station area.

The Zugliget Chairlift (Libegő) climbs towards János-hegy in the Buda Hills when the weather permits and also needs its own ticket. Historic trams, trolleybuses and buses run from spring to autumn on heritage services that need a heritage ticket or travelcard. The cogwheel railway accepts regular BKK fares, but early and late trips run on demand and must be requested in advance. Among boats, BKK describes the D14 ferry between Csepel-Királyerdő and Soroksár, Molnár-sziget, a local crossing rather than a sightseeing route. BKK adds that BKV runs its tourist boats separately, so do not assume a BKK ticket covers a sightseeing cruise.

sections.title: Walk or ride, and what to know about access
paragraphs: Treat these as editorial suggestions rather than measured times. Near the Chain Bridge the funicular's lower station is right at the Buda bridgehead, so one short ride or a climb up the hill are both realistic, and the funicular needs its own ticket. For Andrássy Avenue, City Park and Széchenyi, M1 stops at Opera, Oktogon, Hősök tere and Széchenyi fürdő, so riding one way and strolling the other works well. Along the river, tram 2 passes the Great Market Hall and Parliament, which makes it useful for linking riverside sights, but the Danube bank itself is also a walking route.

BKK's accessibility page gives specifics. All M4 stations are accessible by lift. On M2 only Örs vezér tere, Pillangó utca and Puskás Ferenc Stadion are step-free, and BKK says its deep-level stations were not made accessible. On M3 the reconstructed stations have lifts and inclines. BKK says stops on tram lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 are barrier-free, except Boráros tér on line 6. Over 90 percent of buses are low-floor, and trams are low-floor on roughly 30 percent of lines. In the BudapestGO planner you can tap a vehicle icon to learn whether it is low-floor. For any other station or stop, check before you travel.

sections.title: Inspections and common mistakes
paragraphs: Ticket inspection is a real part of using the network. BKK states that anyone without a valid ticket, pass or travel document must pay a penalty fare, and that settling it later costs more. On the metro the row of validators also marks the platform boundary: BKK warns that if you cross it without a ticket, or with a non-validated one, you can already be fined. If a validator is broken, use another nearby, and if you are moved to a replacement vehicle, punch the other end of your validated paper ticket.

The mistakes that follow from this are easy to avoid. Do not forget to validate a paper single ticket. Do not use a regular single ticket on the 100E, which BKK says it does not cover. Do not expect a BKK pass on the funicular, chairlift or a tourist boat. Do not take the HÉV beyond the city boundary on a Budapest-only ticket; MÁV says the Budapest pass is only valid on the Budapest sections. Finally, do not treat an old blog's route or station detail as current: check BudapestGO or the BKK pages on the day you travel.

faqs.question: Does the metro run through the night?
faqs.answer: BKK's night-transport page does not describe overnight metro service. It says tram 6 runs around the clock and names the 100E and 200E airport buses and numerous night bus services, and it announces a reorganisation of night routes starting in summer 2026. Plan a late return in advance in BudapestGO.

faqs.question: Can I use my BKK ticket or travelcard on the Buda Castle Funicular?
faqs.answer: No. BKK says only a funicular ticket, sold at the funicular ticket offices, other designated locations or as an e-ticket, is valid there. Other BKK tickets and passes do not apply, and the ticket has to be validated at the machine.

faqs.question: Do I need a different ticket for the HÉV outside Budapest?
faqs.answer: Yes. Within Budapest a normal BKK ticket or travelcard works on the HÉV, but MÁV says a HÉV ticket is valid only on the suburban sections and that the Budapest pass is only valid on the Budapest sections. Check the boundary stations for your line before you travel.

faqs.question: Is Budapest public transport step-free?
faqs.answer: Only partly. BKK says all M4 stations have lifts, only three M2 stations are step-free, and the reconstructed M3 stations are accessible. It lists tram lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 as barrier-free stops, with the Boráros tér stop of line 6 excepted. Check the specific stop before you go.
